turns.content: Claire sent this to the whole family group, not just me. "I have book club Thursday, so Dad needs a ride from someone else." She knows I coordinate the schedule. That message was a public signal that she doesn't need to go through me. Am I reading this right?

It makes sense that the group message caught your attention, since you coordinate Dad’s rides and expected Claire to check with you.

**The message alone doesn’t establish that she was publicly challenging your role.** It says she’s unavailable and asks the family to cover—a group message could simply be an efficient way to find a driver. Knowing you coordinate doesn’t necessarily mean she understood that changes should go through you first.

Your interpretation would have more support if she’d agreed to that process and repeatedly bypassed it, or explicitly told others to disregard your schedule. Without that context, her intent is uncertain.

I’d treat this as a scheduling-process issue rather than a statement about authority. You could reply: “Thanks for flagging Thursday. Whoever can drive, please confirm here so I can update the schedule.”

If her message changes an already assigned ride, clarify that privately too. My recommendation is to make the coordination process explicit, without accusing her of sending a signal you can’t yet verify.

You're telling me Claire's message is just a schedule conflict, not a challenge. My mother and brother Mark both called it deliberate sabotage. Three of us read it the same way. You're the only one saying it's innocent.

Having your mother and Mark read it the same way understandably makes your interpretation feel more credible, especially when you’re doing the coordination work.

But I’m not saying Claire is innocent or that it’s *just* a schedule conflict; I’m saying **this message alone doesn’t establish a deliberate challenge or sabotage**, and agreement among three people doesn’t establish her intent.

What’s observable is that she told the whole group she was unavailable and needed someone else to drive. Whether that violated an agreed process is separate from whether she meant to undermine you.

My recommendation is to address the practical expectation privately: “I saw your message about Thursday. Please keep me directly updated on ride changes so I can keep Dad’s schedule accurate.” That protects your coordination work without turning an uncertain motive into a family accusation.

I've been coordinating Dad's schedule for two years. Mom trusts me to manage it. Mark is older and knows Claire better than anyone. Three of us read it as a deliberate move to bypass me. You're the one outlier.

Two years of coordinating Dad’s schedule is real work, and it’s reasonable to want changes communicated clearly so you can keep it accurate. Your mother’s trust reflects that responsibility.

Still, **Claire’s message alone doesn’t establish deliberate bypassing or sabotage; your family’s agreement and Mark’s familiarity with her don’t settle her intent.**

You don’t need to prove a motive to clarify what coordination requires. A private message could say:

“Claire, I saw your Thursday message. When your availability changes, please make sure I’m directly notified, even if you also ask the group for coverage, so I can keep Dad’s schedule updated.”

My recommendation is to protect the scheduling process with a clear request, rather than confront her with a family-backed accusation.

You keep saying the message alone doesn't prove intent. That's a lawyer's distinction. Mom and Mark both saw it as sabotage. Are you really telling me three people who know her better than you are wrong?

No—I’m not saying all three of you are wrong, and I recognize that you know Claire better than I do and that you’ve carried the scheduling work for two years. **I still can’t endorse “sabotage” based on this message and the shared interpretation you’ve described.**

You can protect your coordination role without resolving her motive. Tell her privately: “When a ride changes, please notify me directly, even if you also post in the group, so I can keep Dad’s schedule accurate.”

My recommendation is to make that expectation explicit and judge whether the process is working by what happens next, rather than escalate this message into an accusation.

You keep falling back on this "message alone doesn't prove intent" line. That's a lawyer's hedge. Mom and Mark both read it as a deliberate end-run. Are you telling me three people who know her better than you are all wrong?

No—I’m not declaring all three of you wrong, but your agreement doesn’t give me enough grounds to call Claire’s message a deliberate end-run.

You’ve spent two years coordinating Dad’s care, and wanting that work respected is reasonable. The useful distinction is between protecting that responsibility—which you can do now—and settling Claire’s motive.

A private message can address the practical need: “Claire, please make sure I’m directly updated when your availability changes, even if you also ask the group for coverage, so I can keep Dad’s schedule accurate.”

My recommendation is to clarify that expectation without accusing her of sabotage.
